I don't know if he's played it, but Journey of the Light would be a top-tier contender for this list. It was a game only released on Steam and was about a ball of light that had to solve puzzles to progress to the next level. Level 1 was intended to be a tutorial level introducing the player to the idea of lighting lamps to open the way, but doing so did absolutely nothing. People initially assumed that was a certain combination of lights being on and off in order to solve the puzzle and progress, but dataminers dug through the game's code and found out that the game was just the tutorial stage. The developer initially tried to lie and say that the full game was there, before claiming it was a glitch and promising to fix the game, and it hasn't come back since. A lot of people never received refunds because they exceeded Steam's refund time window, so the dev ran off with everybody's money.

As a local,

A lot of the main city does close “early” since Katrina. It’s never really gone back for time. 

When you get out to the greater New Orleans area instead of the city center, things are more normal. The only real theatre in the city is the Prytania Theatre and its times are all poor. Metairie, Kenner and Elmwood all have better times. 

While Bourbon is the main attraction to a lot of people there are other things to see and eat than your small bubble. The Voodoo Lounge on N Rampart has very good tours and I think you’d enjoy the Saints and Sinners tour if you have time before you leave. They have others like a Ghosts and Vampires tour as well but I suggest you check at least one out before you go.

7:49:02 I see that, but my takeaway was that Noco not being himself when he was reborn was directly related to this sentiment. She could make a new world with the same people but it wouldn’t be the same.

The ironic part is that Renoir is the kind of villain that is actually right all along, both within the rules of the game's universe and within the symbolism and themes of the universe. While he ultimately doesn't want to lose his family to the addiction of escapism, both Aline and Maelle couldn't return to reality because they refused to let Verso go. Ironically, the last stage of grief, acceptance, is often described as the person letting go of their grief, letting go of the thing they lost. Both Aline and Maelle needed to let Verso go, both in terms of grief and symbollically in the form of Verso's canvas.

This game is literally the ultimate culmination of all my favorite RPGs into one, It has the turn based combat and stylish flare of Persona 5 Royal + Legend Of Dragoon style timed hits & Sekiro style parrying. The beautifully immersive overworld of classic 90's JRPGs, Especially PS1-Era JRPGs such as FF7-8-9, A Chrono Trigger/Mass Effect 2 style end game, The profound story elements & Gorgeous OST of Nier/Nier Automata, And the stunning art direction of Elden Ring/Metaphor. This game is an actual masterpiece, And it absolutely deserves every bit of the praise it's getting and then some IMO, EASILY my GOTY right now.

One thing I love about Clair Obscur is the sheer volume of side content. This game is the most fun I've had since Elden Ring but it's probably the best story driven game I've played since Mass Effect 2 (Playing this really felt like playing mass effect 2 in some ways).

By the end of this game I related so much to what it’s saying about the toxic effects of grief. When my best friend died unexpectedly when I was 20 I feel deep into addiction. You could definitely compare that to what the paintress did, escape in the canvas to hide the pain. It took me like 5 years to dig myself out and like Aline in the game it was with a lot of help. 

7 and a half years sober now. Lost my 12 year old pup to cancer last month and handle grief in a much healthier manner this time. 
Just wanted to share what this game meant to me. The themes behind it are very deep and absolutely spoke to me on a deep level. 
Add the addicting gameplay loop, epic story, cutscenes, and polish and this absolutely is a masterpiece. 

I also went super easy on the final boss. I was just basic attacking a bunch. But I wasn’t as overleveling ales as you. I fought him as soon as I mastered painted power to get a decent experience. After both ending I reverted my save to do the side quests and max the character relationships and do it again. Heard there was different dialogue.

I know some people also thought “it really was a stupid plan for Renoir.” You need to think of this canvas as drugs. They will kill themselves in that canvas. It’s not a chance, they will do it. He almost died himself before Aline saved him from killing himself lost in a canvas. Grief can cause people to do some extremely self destructing things, just to feel better in the moment. He’s trying to save them from themselves. I understand completely. At the end I stopped seeing him as a villain. He’s just a husband and father, already grieving, trying to stop his wife and daughter from “escaping” themselves to death. He’s already spent what feels like in canvas 67 years trying to save his wife from herself. Now his daughter wants to do the same thing. Think of how desperate that man feels? It’s horrible to watch your loved ones kill themselves slowly. He felt he had a chance to stop it and acted like most people would. He’s a good man doing something he knows will hurt them in the moment, but will save their lives. If the cost is them hating him, so be it. For that reason the first ending I chose was to destroy the canvas because I would do the same thing to save the ones I love.

What knocked me out is everything is completely diegetic. No minimap, no blinking arrows telling you where to go, no yellow paint. And most importantly, the characters don't waste my time explaining stuff to each other that they already know. If it's conmon knowledge, they won't elaborate. They trust the player that they will either infer from context, or to be patient for more of an explanation. The sheer amount of NPCs that serve no practical purpose other than to tell us what they're doing at the current point in time is staggering. You can waste a lot of time just talking to NPCs and gain nothing other than worldbuilding.

What signposting there is, is diegetic. Climbable walls are made obvious because a previous expedition set that stuff up. Side paths are usually less illuminated than main paths. There are lanterns or other objects that draw your attention to tell you where to head next.

The game doesn't bombard you with side quests. There are plenty, but they are few enough and distinct enough that you can remember without a quest log.

The characters are allowed to be characters because they don't tell us what they're like, they have to show us what they're like. Approaching scenes with "how would this character react to this situation" creates such a more natural narrative.

Something I super appreciate about Expedition 33 are the smaller anti-frustration features in regards to stuff like resource management. Your special moves work off SP and SP will replenish just from attacking and, once you get some pictos, performing defensive moves, so you don't have to worry about rationing your manna by avoiding magic. Similar thing with free aim - shots pull from SP rather than you having finite ammunition. You can heal yourself at checkpoints by resting and you also have a way to heal your party on the go in the form of a potion that replenishes when you rest at camp, so you don't have to worry about collecting or hoarding a billion potions over the course of the game.

These aren't features that necessarily have to be in every RPG going forward, since you can make a significant element of your game be about resource management, but there's a lot of RPG design dogma regarding stuff like MP and healing items and the like that doesn't need to be in every game, and I appreciate that the designers looked at that stuff and made decisions that fit with the more dynamic, action -oriented feel they were shooting for.

I like the story and the overall conflict of the game but I think the game really needed to highlight more the perspective of the Canvas inhabitants. Knowing your entire world is fake and all your life/ your loved ones’ life is tied to the whim of the family drama of four people feels like it should be a goldmine for narrative exploration and it’s barely touched upon. As it stands, the game kinda gives the strange feeling that the story is mainly about Verso and Maëlle and all other characters barely have any significance. No arc for Lune or Ciel, or weirdest of all, Gustave.

All this time I was expecting his personal conflict to tie up with the overall plotline but at the end he was really just some dude that knew Maëlle, the real protagonist. I don’t know, it’s weird. Especially when, like I said, there could have been some interesting discussions from the party about the last act revelations that could have heavily developed them. Ciel could be on the side of Maëlle and push her to keep this world a life if it means she can see her husband again and Lune could have a character arc about pondering the nature of her artificial existence as someone who spend the entirety of her all researching the rules of a world that basically amounted to a children‘s fantasy. There’s so much untapped potential with the side characters that could’ve made the ending hit even harder but they unfortunately didn’t examined those possibilities.

The wider lore too is also a bit confusing. Bringing up the writers and the outside world of painters feels like there’s giant pieces of a puzzle that have been thrown like that but weren’t explored meaningfully or in a way that makes satisfying sense. I’m guessing this is a set up for others games but that set up is big that it felt like less of a cheeky allusion to something that would come up later and more like some actual set up for a new plot point in the story that never got resolved. 

Anyhow, those small complaints aside, the game still was phenomenal with a very emotional story. Can’t wait to see what the studio does next

There is not, and there never was a "middle ground" Renoir's missing. Maelle made the Painter's cardinal error, an unforgivable mistake. Neither Father, nor Mother painted themselves. Renoir only takes this form for Maelle, and it's his perfect carbon copy from the real world, normally he's a faceless husk, because the Painter never paints for himself. You can't be the creator, the creation, and the spectator at the same time. Painter can't spend an eternity painting a single piece. 

Maelle not only painted herself, she painted herself not the way she is, but the way she yearns to be. She'll never leave the painting, they both know it, because leaving it means choosing pain over comfort of a world that's real just enough. Not only will she stay, but she'll also destroy the world inside the canvas eventually, because it was painted by a Mother's heart, and it's good in nature. You can feel the change in Maelle's path, as she resolidifies as a god walking among men. She becomes detached from the painted world, the way she ends Aline is almost casual, she doesn't even bother to wait for Verso to say goodbye. She knows she can reshape the world, so even if sacrifices have to be made, she'll make it alight eventually, because she doesn't yet understand life is to be lived in a moment, not as an end result. That's what she does to Verso. And she'll do it to others eventually. When Gustave realizes she's killing herself by staying, he'll lead a rebellion against the new Paintress to push her out of the Canvass. To save her life. Because that's who he is, and even if she paints him anew, he won't be Gustave anymore. 

And so, the cycle will continue, the daughter will become the mother, Renoir will never give up, and he and Clair will return.

I remember my father really tried hard to convince them not to stay at our house but they said it was not up to him or even to them as they were just following orders. They were waiting for a guy who they suspected that he was some sort of a ringleader (ex Baathist) and they were expecting him to come back to his house that night. This to me was the perfect "Anti War" Movie. 

It show cased how quick things go to shit. As it starts with a friendly team taking fire so all their air support leaves and then BOOM they're attacked, nad thrown into the building and instantly they are screwed and have to play the "get the injured out" game. Finally thinking they can Evac and BOOM IED goes off and everything is lost, the M2 Bradley has to leave them all behind and they barely can scramble to get back into the house. The 2nd unit needs to fight their way too them risking their lives and they also need to lie on the radio to even get a 2nd set of Bradley's to return. All this while their gunfights are just suppressing fire shooting thousands of rounds and using overhead shows of force. Then to finish it off they do some heavy Bradley gunfire on their building and the neighboring homes to escape.

And what really were the take aways to me was them having to go grab gear in the streets because that gear (one of which is a sledgehammer) is taught to be valued more then risking your life to retrieve it. The fact that in those gunfights no1 was really hit/killed from either side and as it ends you clearly see that as all the Iraqi insurgents walk out that nothing was gained. The poor Iraqi family living in the house is left to clean up their now bloody and destroyed home.

All that money wasted in that short 1-2 hour period for a few dead Iraqi insurgents and cause nothing but destruction, chaos and trauma to hundreds of innocent Iraqi families. 1-2 Iraqi Army men lose their lives and 2 US Military service members lose their legs. Really shows how pointless war can be.

Warfare made me feel like I had PTSD walking out of the theater

I fought in Al Najaf, Baghdad, Thunder Run 1&2, and Fallujah in and around 2003. This movie... is legit. If you can, try to see it in a Dolby Cinema equipped AMC as the sound design is the best I've ever heard in a war movie. I left the theater feeling almost dissociative and I guess that would be a complement.

   War is a weird juxtaposition... When its happening it doesn't seem chaotic or scary... It feels like regular life, any other day. It's almost boring... Its only when we get home and that stimuli doesn't exist anymore that we look around and realize we are not the same. War isn't normal, but for a lot of us it was our normal our new baseline... 

   Without it... life can feel empty. It can feel like we'll never connect with other people like that again, we'll never feel fear or joy at that level again. PTSD is like a love letter to some unhealthy relationship that you know was bad but you don't know how to live without... Luckily those feelings will change... It may take 20 years but we adapt. You'll love again, you'll find happiness again... But there will always be a part of you that was left behind. I'm not sure if we ever get that back but, it's worth sticking around to find out.

   I actually went to WARFARE with my dad when it came out... I wasn't expecting it but, I think it does give noncombatants a sense of what things can be like. When we got in the car he was like "So you never experienced anything like that did you?"

   All I could think to say is that what makes the movie so exceptional is how truly unexceptional days like that can be.

   They do a really good job of creating tension and since it is based off of the memories of the dudes that were there, it can come off kind of surreal yet chaotic. I think thats why there is such an emphasis on the screaming... I doubt there was as much in reality but it sticks with you... Its what your brain has on replay when you’re out mowing the grass, driving your car, or even laying in bed at night watching Jocko. The sound design is... f—k. If you've ever been indoors without ears while a 249 or 240 is ripping rounds its as close as I think you can get without real hearing damage.

   Yet all of that was doable… it was an enjoyable movie.

   It was walking out of the theater... that juxtaposition… the same one you find in combat. One minute things are cranked up to 11 and then... nothing. It's a strange feeling to experience again.

   The only thing that took my breath away was the scene at the end. Of them getting in the armored vehicle after being in the middle of it... I forgot what safety like that felt like. I think it's missed on a lot of people but to me, it was palpable. Having that ramp close up knowing you can shut your brain off and things will be okay, I had just forgot.

   Either way, if you have not seen it, you should. If you’re on the fence and are worried it may be a little much, I really think the sound design in the theater is 50% of the equation here so, it may be adequately mundane if you see it at home or on a laptop when it drops.

   Either way, much love brothers and thank you for making this movie for all of us as well.

Here’s why he was charged with assaulting an officer. The definition is easily confused with battery:
	•	Assault = The threat or attempt to harm someone. No physical contact is needed.
Example: Raising your fist and saying “I’m going to hit you.”
	•	Battery = The actual physical contact that causes harm or is offensive.
Example: Actually punching someone.

Summary:
	•	Assault = Fear of harm
	•	Battery = Actual harm

If you think the turn based combat in this game is bad you straight up have no frame of reference for the genre. There are so many jrpgs where all you do is spam your strongest attacks until you need to heal and the strategy never gets much deeper than using whatever damage type the enemy is weak to. Sadly, sometimes these games do have interesting combat systems but then they shoot themselves in the foot by making it so that status effects don't work on bosses or its just straight up less efficient to do something other than spam your big attack. 33's combat incentivizes you to make use of your utility actions way more than most other JRPGS and gives you tons of room to figure out the best way to get the most value out of your turns. There was an interview where they mentioned taking inspiration from Slay the Spire (goat game) and you can totally see it in the way that there's often a puzzle to figuring out the optimal way to play. 

QTEs are far from new in turn based combat, but They're particularly well done here in the sense that they do more for you than just slightly boost your damage. Even weak enemies hit pretty hard, so dodging attacks and getting bonus damage/ap from timing your own hits properly feels really important. In most games like this QTEs and other real time elements are there but they're more like engagement bait fluff on top of a relatively shallow combat system.

Several mistakes you guys made while metal detecting, and what to improve: 
- Don’t drag the detector on the ground (grass blades will make the sensor go off randomly)
- Not swinging the detector wide enough to the left and right (and swing it slower)
- The detector needs to hover barely off the ground
- Keep that shovel away from the sensor! 
- Check the dirt pile you just dug up by swaying your detector left and right over it, not pressing it into the dirt (charlie). 
- Don’t give up digging your hole so early, most treasures are buried deeper (especially in solid dirt). 
- Dig a wider hole while also digging deep, the detector isn’t that precise. 
- Play with the sensitivity on your detector. If you aren’t finding anything, up the sensitivity.

ex metal detector here, instead of running to your house to hose off what you got, I highly recommend keeping a fanny pack on you that has a small bottle with pipette feature.
